what: NIQ measures what consumers buy. It collects sales data from retailers and from household panels, then sells manufacturers and retailers the picture of what sold, where, at what price and against which competitor. It was formerly the Nielsen consumer measurement business.
customers: Consumer goods manufacturers deciding what to make, price and promote, and retailers managing their shelves and assortments, across many countries.
money: Subscription access to retail sales data, market share measurement and analytics tools.
moat: Retail measurement is a natural near-monopoly: the value of the data depends on covering most of the market, so one provider that aggregates data from most retailers is worth far more than two with half each. Brand managers also compare market share against history, which means switching provider breaks the comparability of years of data.
risks: Debt of $3.9B against $518.8M of cash is enormous relative to a $5.0B market value, a legacy of the private equity ownership before listing.
A trailing net loss of $117.0M, and last year’s net margin was negative 8.4% — interest expense is consuming the operating profit.
The company listed recently and has revenue history only from 2023, so there is no public record through a downturn.
Consumer goods manufacturers under margin pressure cut research budgets, and measurement subscriptions are a visible line item.
Thirteen analysts average a $23.04 target against a $16.79 price, a 37% gap reflecting disagreement about the deleveraging.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $488.6M against a $5.0B market value is a 9.8% yield, and the shares trade at about 10.1 times free cash flow.
Revenue has grown from $3.3B in 2023 to $4.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $4.5B.
Retail measurement is close to a natural monopoly: data is only valuable if it covers most of the market.
Brand managers compare market share against years of history, which makes switching provider break the comparability.
Subscription revenue is recurring and contracted, which makes the revenue base predictable.
watch: Organic revenue growth and net debt relative to EBITDA. The business quality is established; the leverage determines what the equity is worth.
view: Retail measurement is an unusually good business and it comes down to one property: the data is only valuable if it covers most of the market. A provider with sales data from most retailers can tell a manufacturer its true market share; a provider with half the market cannot. That makes the business tend toward one dominant supplier per market, and it makes the incumbent extremely hard to displace — particularly because brand managers compare share against years of their own history, and switching provider breaks that comparability permanently.

NIQ has that position in many countries, and the revenue reflects it: $3.3 billion to $4.5 billion trailing, almost all of it recurring subscriptions. That is a high-quality revenue base, and $489 million of free cash flow against a $5.0 billion market value shows the underlying economics are strong.

The problem is $3.9 billion of debt against $519 million of cash. That came from the private equity ownership that preceded the listing, and it is why a business generating $489 million of free cash flow reports a $117 million net loss — interest expense consumes the operating profit. The equity is therefore a leveraged claim on a good business rather than a direct one, and that distinction governs everything about how it should be sized.

So the question is arithmetic rather than strategy. If organic revenue keeps growing and the free cash flow goes to debt reduction, the value transferred to shareholders over several years is large, and at 10.1 times free cash flow the starting point is undemanding. If consumer goods manufacturers under margin pressure start cutting research budgets — and measurement subscriptions are a visible, cuttable line item — the deleveraging stalls. With a public record only from 2023 and no experience of a downturn, the thirteen analysts at $23.04 are modelling rather than observing. Organic growth and net debt to EBITDA are the two numbers.
bull: A near-monopoly measurement franchise keeps growing organically while $489 million of annual free cash flow deleverages $3.9 billion of debt into a cheap equity.
bear: Consumer goods clients cut research budgets, organic growth stalls, and leverage at nearly eight times free cash flow leaves the equity with no cushion.
